title: Edge DNS stabilization and rollback observations
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures observed friction points and pragmatic runbook edits from the Feb 2025 edge DNS degradation incident where multi-region traffic shifts and DNS TTL changes were used to evacuate an affected POP. The goal is a lightweight, executable checklist for on-call engineers and a set of telemetry checks we can include in the runbook.

Summary of event (short):
- 2025-02-19 09:12 UTC: Edge POP in eu-west-1 started seeing intermittent egress failures to upstream ISP (packet loss spikes, BGP withdraws).
- 09:18 UTC: Canary latency and 5xx rates increased for requests routed through that POP.
- 09:27 UTC: Automated routing policy reduced weight to 0.4 for eu-west-1; TTL remained 60.
- 09:35 UTC: Operators attempted rapid DNS TTL reduction to 10s and issued a weighted traffic shift to adjacent regions.
- 09:42 UTC: kvcache warmup failed for some prefixes; burst of cold-start latency observed in failover regions.
- 10:05 UTC: Rollback executed after discovering DNS provider rate-limited updates; final stabilization at 10:30 UTC.

Key observations (what surprised us):
- DNS provider behavior: The provider applied per-zone update-rate limits that were not surfaced in our runbook. Bulk TTL reductions were queued and applied over ~20 minutes, negating our intent.
- Negative coupling of TTL and DNS-based routing: Lowering TTL helps failover agility, but when your provider rate-limits updates, the partial application of TTL changes created inconsistent client views (some clients stuck at old TTLs while others adopted new ones).
- kvcache rehydration cost: Pre-seeding kvcache from the source region to targets works for many prefixes, but our preseed step missed several ephemeral user-session prefixes (session tokens), producing a secondary spike of backend RPS and latency.
- Monitoring granularity: Per-POP dashboards did not have a clear visualization of in-flight DNS TTL status or provider update queue length; operators were guessing TTL propagation state.

Immediate tactical changes (to apply now):
- Add an explicit check in the runbook that queries DNS provider API for pending updates and rate-limit status before attempting mass TTL changes. Command example: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $DNS_TOKEN" https://api.dnsprovider.example.com/zones/{zone}/update-queue
- If provider rate-limits are in effect, prefer traffic weight shifts via the control-plane router (weighted LB) instead of TTL changes.
- Extend kvcache preseed to include session-prefixes and short-lived keys; add a dry-run verification that counts seeded prefixes vs expected prefix list.
- Add a temporary protection: when performing large traffic shifts, set a graceful ingress-shed policy that caps failover-region concurrency by 20% above normal to avoid backend saturation.

Runbook draft (practical checklist for an SRE handling a similar event):
1) Triage and confirm scope:
   - Check SLO/alert: run this PromQL to get per-POP 5xx rate: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="edge",status=~"5..",pop=~".*"}[5m])) by (pop) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="edge",pop=~".*"}[5m])) by (pop)
   - Verify BGP/peering: run BGP feed query and peering metrics for the POP.
2) Query DNS provider for pending operations and rate limits:
   - API: GET /zones/{zone}/update-queue and /rate-limits (example above).
   - If queued updates > 0 or rate-limit close to threshold, do NOT issue mass TTL change.
3) Orchestrate rotating weight shift via control plane:
   - Step weights in 10% increments every 2 minutes; monitor latency and 5xx after each step.
   - Use the router command: rwctl route adjust --pop eu-west-1 --weight -10 --dry-run && rwctl route apply --pop eu-west-1 --weight -10
4) Preseed KV cache to target POPs:
   - Run preseed job with additional flag --include-session-prefixes.
   - Verification: check seeded_count >= expected_count (query from preseed-monitoring job).
5) Monitor for secondary effects:
   - Backend RPC latency, DB connection queue length, and provisioned GPU pools for model serving.
6) If traffic shift fails or provider blocks DNS changes, roll back to previous stable weights and escalate to network team.

Rollback criteria (when to unwind a shift):
- Immediate rollback if any of these occur within 10 minutes of a shift:
  - failover-region P95 latency > 3x baseline AND sustained increase in backend CPU > 40%
  - sustained 5xx rate above SLO (0.5%)
  - clear evidence of DNS provider throttling causing uneven client state
- Partial rollback (reduce step) if transient degradation but not severe saturation.

Operational telemetry to add to dashboards (specific metrics/visuals):
- DNS provider: queued updates, per-zone update throttle, last-applied-update timestamp (New panel).
- Client resolution mapping: estimated fraction of clients still resolving to old TTL (approximation from resolver logs).
- Preseed coverage: seeded prefixes vs expected list, and a small sample of session-prefix miss rate.
- Failover-region admission rate vs provisioned concurrency (heatmap).

Post-incident tasks / action items (owners assigned):
- Alex Chen: add provider-rate-limit check and sample curl command to runbook (due 2025-03-10).
- Priya Kapoor: implement seeded-prefix verification job and dashboard panel (due 2025-03-17).
- Daniel Ortiz: contact DNS provider to ask for SLA/rate-limit visibility and request a higher burst allowance for incident windows (created ticket DNS-2025-02).
- Marta Silva: update canary-weight automation to pause on >20% backend CPU spike (due 2025-03-24).

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- Can we negotiate a provider feature: atomic zone TTL push that guarantees uniform TTL application across their edge?
- Explore a hybrid approach: small TTL reductions (e.g., 60->30) combined with weight shifts instead of aggressive TTL=10 changes.
- Should we build a DNS propagation simulator to model client-side caching across common resolvers? (quick prototype idea: sample from Chrome/Firefox resolver TTL behaviors and simulate propagation with rate-limited update application)

Lessons learned (concise):
- Treat DNS provider behavior as part of the system; assume update-rate limits and design playbooks to query and respect them.
- Preseed kvcache more aggressively for session-like prefixes; rehydrate verification is a must.
- Prefer control-plane weight adjustments when provider-side operations are unreliable.

Appendix: useful commands & queries
- Check DNS queue: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $DNS_TOKEN" https://api.dnsprovider.example.com/zones/rdw-prod.example.com/update-queue
- Example router adjust (dry-run): rwctl route adjust --pop eu-west-1 --weight -20 --dry-run
- PromQL 5xx by pop: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=~"edge.*",status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (pop) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=~"edge.*"}[5m])) by (pop)
- KV preseed check (pseudo): curl -s https://preseed-monitoring.internal/seeded_count?pop=eu-west-1

Rough timeline annex (detailed timestamps captured in incident log):
- 09:12 UTC: first packet loss alert
- 09:18 UTC: canary latency up 150%
- 09:27 UTC: automated router weight reduction triggered (policy)
